card.hook: Picture 829.8 metres of tower trying to squeeze into your phone screen, with a crowd of other phones doing the same thing. That's the Burj Khalifa, and it's worth the elbow room.
card.stand_here: Stand on Souk Al Bahar Bridge, the small footbridge over Burj Khalifa Lake on the Souk Al Bahar side. Face the tower so it rises behind the Dubai Fountain, with the lake in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the tower, fountain and lake in one frame. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight, with the lake in the bottom third of the frame.
card.best_time: Arrive early for the evening fountain shows, because the bridge gets very crowded. In daylight, early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the tower.
card.selfie_here: Take it on Souk Al Bahar Bridge, the classic spot where the tower sits behind the fountain and lake. Turn to face away from the tower, use the front camera at 0.5x, and let the tower rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a full-tower photo of you, ask a passer-by to stand at the southern end of the Burj Park island (over the footbridge from the Dubai Mall waterfront) so the whole tower fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is free but very busy at show times. Fountain shows and Burj Park access can change, so check before you go.
card.challenge: Take three frames at three different distances, then pick the one where the tower stands straightest.
card.good_to_know: The Burj Khalifa opened in January 2010 as the centrepiece of Downtown Dubai. Skidmore, Owings & Merrill gave it a Y-shaped floor plan, with three wings stepping up to a slim spire. That tapering shape is why it looks like one clean vertical line from a good spot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Souk Al Bahar Bridge, the small footbridge over Burj Khalifa Lake on the Souk Al Bahar side. Face the tower so it rises behind the Dubai Fountain, with the lake in front of you.

card.hook: From the ground, Palm Jumeirah is a nice island with a lot of hotels. It only turns into a palm tree when you're way up high, and that's the shot everyone comes for.
card.stand_here: Stand at the glass barrier on the open-air terrace of The View at The Palm, in the Palm Tower, about 240 m up. Face out over the island so the crescent, the fronds and the trunk are laid out below you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole palm shape into one frame, crescent included. Then try 1x for a tidier skyline, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Dubai Marina and the distant towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the trunk up with a vertical line, so the fronds spread evenly on both sides.
card.best_time: Sunset is the time guides recommend, but those slots cost more and sell out, so book ahead. After the light fades, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the barrier to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the glass barrier on Level 52 of The View at The Palm, with the island spread out behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so the palm fits over your shoulder, and hold the phone close to the glass to cut reflections. If you've got an upgraded ticket, the open-air terrace on Level 54 has no glass barriers, so there are no reflections at all.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks need prior approval from The View at The Palm before you go in, so check with them first. Keep your phone clear of the glass barriers instead of holding it out over the railing.
card.challenge: Get the whole crescent in the frame, the trunk lined up straight, and your own grin in the corner. That's three things, and you can do it.
card.good_to_know: Building began in June 2001, and the Dutch dredging company Van Oord did the work. As of 2024 there are around 30 hotels on the trunk and crescent. Drone flying over the Palm is heavily restricted, so the terrace is your realistic way to get an aerial-style shot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the glass barrier on the open-air terrace of The View at The Palm, in the Palm Tower, about 240 m up. Face out over the island so the crescent, the fronds and the trunk are laid out below you.

card.hook: Most people shoot the Burj Al Arab on its own. The better picture has a souk arch around it, with the glowing white sail sitting in the opening like a painting in a frame.
card.stand_here: Head to the outdoor canal walkways or open-air dining terraces at Souk Madinat Jumeirah. Face the hotel in the distance and line it up in the gap of an arch.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the arches, the water and the hotel together. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the sail. Use 0.5x only if you're right next to an arch and want it to frame the scene.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the hotel, then slide the brightness to darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the sail, and turn on gridlines to keep the tower on a straight vertical line.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk usually works well, when the sky softens and the hotel's lighting starts to show. Check on the day, as conditions vary.
card.selfie_here: Try the free public sand of Jumeirah public beach beside Jumeirah Beach Hotel. Turn your back to the water so the sail-shaped hotel is across the water behind you, use the front camera (and 0.5x if your front camera has it) and tilt the phone up a little so the whole tower fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On the boardwalk in front of the Waldorf Astoria on Palm Jumeirah, ask a passer-by to shoot across the water at the hotel while you stand in the foreground.
card.rules_and_safety: The hotel is private and its island isn't open to walk-ins, and most of the shoreline near it is private too. On the public beach, ask before including other beachgoers in your shot. Beach access rules may have changed, so check local signs.
card.challenge: Take three frames at different zoom levels, then pick the one where the arches and the tower balance best. Bonus points if nobody's thumb sneaks in.
card.good_to_know: The Burj Al Arab opened on 1 December 1999 and is about 321 m tall. Its shape is meant to recall the sail of a dhow, and the translucent facade is lit up at night. The island sits roughly 280 m offshore, joined to land by a private curving bridge. The hotel is currently closed for renovation until 31 October 2027, so check what the exterior looks like before planning a special trip.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the outdoor canal walkways or open-air dining terraces at Souk Madinat Jumeirah. Face the hotel in the distance and line it up in the gap of an arch.

card.hook: You walk in for a quick snap and end up eye to eye with a 24-metre dinosaur skeleton, with sharks swimming past around the corner. This place is a whole day out, and your camera roll is about to get very busy.
card.stand_here: Head inside The Dubai Mall and walk to the middle of the building, where the phone icon sits. Then find an open spot with a clear view up or along the length of a hall, and face down the hall.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for tall atriums and big open halls, then 1x for shopfronts and people. Try 2x or 5x for details like the Dubai Dino or fish in the aquarium (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with pillars or shop fronts, because tall interiors look tilted very easily.
card.best_time: Quieter hours mean cleaner shots with fewer people in the frame. If you want the Dubai Fountain outside too, wait until after dark for the lights and music.
card.selfie_here: Try the Dubai Steel Heart, the mirrored heart sculpture outside near Burj Khalifa Lake, which is placed so the tower sits behind it. Leave by the exit nearest the Waterfall Wall, switch to the front camera, and keep the Burj Khalifa over your shoulder. The covered bridge between Souk Al Bahar and the Dubai Mall waterfront is another good one, with the tower above the Dubai Fountain. Reviewers call its centred view good for selfies without photobombers, and zoom 0.5x helps fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Walk the footbridge from the Dubai Mall waterfront to the southern end of Burj Park island, hand your phone to a passer-by, and ask for a wide shot so the whole tower fits from base to tip.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal smartphone photos and selfies generally need no approval. Avoid photographing identifiable people without their consent, and note that some attractions inside, like the aquarium, are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the Dubai Dino and get a shot where you look tiny and he looks enormous, with your grid lines keeping everything nice and straight.
card.good_to_know: The Dubai Mall opened on 4 November 2008 and now has over 1,200 shops. It drew a record 105 million visitors in 2023. The Dubai Dino is about 24 metres long and over 7 metres high, and the Dubai Aquarium & Underwater Zoo shows more than 300 species of marine animals.

card.hook: Atlantis is so big and so symmetrical that even a quick snap looks like a postcard. Two towers, one huge gap in the middle, and not much else to get wrong.
card.stand_here: Walk to the phone icon on the map, about 180 m south-east of the hotel, and face north-west. Keep your phone level so the towers don't lean.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view. If both wings won't fit, tap 0.5x. For the roofline and the upper part of the building, try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they stand up straight.
card.best_time: Morning or the hour before sunset gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows. After dark, try night mode and hold very still for a second or two, with your elbows tucked in or resting on something steady.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone a bit lower and further out. That lets you tuck the hotel in over your shoulder instead of just a patch of sky.
card.rules_and_safety: Atlantis is a private hotel with ticketed attractions like Aquaventure and the Lost Chambers Aquarium, so check the official site before you go to see what the public can enter.
card.challenge: Get both towers in one shot with the edges of the building fully in the frame, and nothing clipped. Bonus points if the gridlines say they're dead straight.
card.good_to_know: Atlantis, The Palm opened on 24 September 2008 and was the first resort built on Palm Jumeirah. It's themed on the myth of Atlantis, with some Arabian touches. The main building is 23 storeys high, with 1,544 rooms split between the East Tower and the West Tower.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the phone icon on the map, about 180 m south-east of the hotel, and face north-west. Keep your phone level so the towers don't lean.

card.hook: Picture a little wooden abra bobbing across Dubai Creek while a whole market of gold glints just up the bank. That's your photo here, and it's a general view, so take a few steps along the bank and check the framing as you go.
card.stand_here: Stand at Deira Old Souk Abra Station on the Dubai Creek bank, where the souk entrance is to the north, about 500 m on foot. Face the water and look across the creek towards the souk district.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the creek and waterfront. Go to 2x-5x to pick out an abra or a shop detail (higher zooms depend on your phone), and use 0.5x at the arched entrance if it's crowded.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the waterline on the lower third, tap the abra, and slide it a touch darker so the sky and water don't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the creek and fewer people at the water's edge. Check the souk's current opening times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Go to the souk entrance (Gate 3) on Old Baladiya Street and stand with the gate behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone slightly low so the entrance sits over your shoulder. The small square inside the souk, with the shop-lined alleys around you, is another spot visitors use for photos.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by near the Gate 3 entrance, where taxis gather nearby, to take your photo with the gate behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask shopkeepers before you photograph their displays. The souk is a working market, so access and rules may change. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch an abra in the bottom third of your frame with a dead-level horizon, then see if you can do it again before it floats out of shot.
card.good_to_know: The Dubai Gold Souk has more than 380 retailers, mostly jewellery traders selling gold, platinum and silver, plus bullion and loose stones. It began informally in the early 1900s, when a handful of merchants set up beside the creek. It once held the world's largest ring, at 64 kg. Renovation has been announced for the near future, so the look may change.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Deira Old Souk Abra Station on the Dubai Creek bank, where the souk entrance is to the north, about 500 m on foot. Face the water and look across the creek towards the souk district.

card.hook: A giant silver ring with Arabic calligraphy cut through it, floating beside a motorway. It looks like a film prop, and it's even better in your photos.
card.stand_here: Stand on the far side of Sheikh Zayed Road, directly opposite the museum. You get there by the Emirates Towers Metro pedestrian crossing. Face the museum, with the twin Emirates Towers framing the view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole ring with the towers around it. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the calligraphy. From the pedestrian bridge at Emirates Towers Metro Station, zoom 0.5x gets more of the skyline and road in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, tap the glowing lettering, then slide the brightness down a little so the lit calligraphy doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go from sunset to blue hour, when the calligraphy is backlit and the sky still has some colour. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a railing or wall.
card.selfie_here: Head to the ground-level plaza in front of the silver calligraphy façade. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and stand so the building fills the frame behind your shoulder. For a quieter shot, try the walkway at the back of the museum, on the side away from the main entrance and Sheikh Zayed Road.
card.ask_someone: At the lookout on the passageway across Sheikh Zayed Road, ask a passer-by to take your photo with the museum behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Never cross Sheikh Zayed Road on foot through the traffic. Use the Emirates Towers Metro pedestrian crossing, and take care at the busy side road on the way to the passageway. Indoors, photos are allowed, but staff may restrict them during some live exhibits and flash may be limited in immersive ones. Check the official site for current opening and closure details.
card.challenge: Keep the whole ring in the frame with a little space around it, then take it again with a tower on one side. Which one do you like more?
card.good_to_know: The calligraphy carries three quotes from Dubai's ruler, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, about the future and innovation. The script was written by the Emirati artist Matar Bin Lahej. The shell is made of 1,024 steel-clad panels, each with its own 3D shape, and the museum opened on 22 February 2022.

card.selfie_here: Head to the pedestrian footbridge opposite the Frame's entrance (the one linking Karama to Zabeel Park) and stand so the Frame fills the background behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and check the map to be sure you've found the right bridge.
card.ask_someone: On the lawn near Gate 4, ask a passer-by to crouch low and angle the phone up, while you stand on the grass in front of the Frame, far enough back that the whole thing fits.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed throughout the Dubai Frame for personal use. Zabeel Park may charge entry, so check before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, line the two gold uprights up with the vertical lines, and see if you can get the Frame standing perfectly straight with a palm tree in front.
card.good_to_know: The Dubai Frame is 150.24 m tall and 95.53 m wide, and it holds the record for the largest frame in the world. It opened in January 2018 and works as an observatory, museum and monument. It was built to show old Dubai (Deira, Umm Hurair and Karama) on one side and the modern towers of Sheikh Zayed Road on the other. Going up is a visitor attraction with limited numbers, so check the official site for entry and tickets.

card.hook: Squint across the water and Dubai Marina's towers stop being separate buildings and turn into one giant glittering wall. That's the shot you're here for, and it works best from a distance.

card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the skyline on the upper line so the water fills the lower two thirds, and keep your phone level so the towers don't lean.
card.best_time: Arrive about 45 minutes before sunset for the best light. Stay on, because 15-20 minutes after sunset the towers light up and look completely different.
card.selfie_here: Head to Marina Walk, on the promenade next to Nando's Café, where the water and skyline frame you nicely. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a little low so the towers rise up over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand up on the pedestrian footbridge near Dubai Marina Mall and shoot down at you, with the waterway and towers behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The promenade is an open public space reached on foot, but check the official site before you go in case of closures or restrictions.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice, once in late afternoon and once after dark, and see if you'd believe it's the same skyline.
card.good_to_know: The canal runs about 3 km along the Gulf shoreline. It was dug out of the desert and filled with water from the Gulf. Ciel Dubai Marina is the tall one at 366 metres, and Cayan Tower is the one with the twist. The Walk at JBR, a 1.7 km promenade, opened in 2008.

card.hook: Picture a wheel so big it makes the Dubai Marina towers look like they're standing behind it politely. That's Ain Dubai, and it's one of those things you only really get when you step back.
card.stand_here: Head to The Beach at JBR and walk to the rock groynes at the western end of the public beachfront. The wheel stands about 700 m across the water, to the north-west, so face across the water to the island.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole wheel with the towers and the sea around it. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot that makes the wheel look even bigger against the skyline.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the wheel on one of the vertical lines, and keep the horizon level so you get lots of open sky and sea around it.
card.best_time: Go at sunset, when the wheel often turns into a silhouette against the sky. The lights after dark are a good second choice.
card.selfie_here: Try the palm-lined walkway at the far end of the Bluewaters promenade, past the Bluewaters Residences apartments, where the wheel looms over the palm trees. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the wheel over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone at the JBR end of the pedestrian bridge to Bluewaters Island to shoot back toward the wheel with you in the frame, ideally in the early evening.
card.rules_and_safety: The beachfront and groynes at JBR are public. The wheel's operating status has changed over time, so check before you go if you're hoping for a ride.
card.challenge: Take the same wheel at three zoom levels, and keep the rocks or the water's edge in the front of every shot so the scale really shows.
card.good_to_know: At 250 m, Ain Dubai has been the world's tallest observation wheel since October 2021, beating the Las Vegas High Roller by 82.4 m. It was designed to carry up to 1,750 people in 48 cabins. Its name means 'eye of Dubai', and it reopened to visitors on 26 December 2024 after closing to the public in 2022.

card.hook: Pale walls, a tower at three corners, two cannons by the gate and flags flapping above them: Al Fahidi Fort practically poses for you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at Al Fahidi Fort, which is the Dubai Museum building. Face the eastern wall with the main gate, then step back until the cannons, flags and towers all fit.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the long fort walls and the open courtyard, and 1x for the gate, cannons and flags. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for the wind tower, cannonballs and the rough coral rock.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the walls and towers up against them so the fort looks nice and straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the pale stone. Check the official site for opening times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Inside the courtyard, stand in front of the wind towers and cannon displays, which a travel guide calls iconic backdrops. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit low so the fort sits over your shoulder. Another good spot is the courtyard just past the exit, with its benches and large dhow.

card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks and flash are stated as prohibited inside the museum, so keep both in your bag. card.challenge: Get a cannon big in the foreground, a flag in the top of the frame, and a tower dead straight on the gridlines.
card.good_to_know: Al Fahidi Fort was built in 1787 and is believed to be the oldest surviving building in Dubai. It's made of coral rock and mortar. The museum opened in 1971 to show traditional life in the emirate.

card.hook: A wooden abra putters across the creek, a lantern glows beside you, and the whole scene feels like it's been staged for your phone. It hasn't. This is just how Dubai Creek works.
card.stand_here: Stand in Al Seef Park, on the creekside promenade along the Al Seef waterfront. Face the water so the old-style buildings and lanterns are close in front of you and the abras cross behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the abras, lanterns and old-style buildings in one frame. Drop to zoom 0.5x for the whole promenade and water, then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single boat or the far bank.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the boat, then drag the slider to make the picture slightly darker so the sky and lights don't wash out.
card.best_time: Come at golden hour, when the light is soft and low. Then stay a little longer, because once the lanterns come on after dusk the same view looks completely different (use night mode and rest your elbows on a railing).
card.selfie_here: Stand on the Al Seef waterfront stretch with your back to the creek, so the water and passing abras are right behind you. Use the front camera, hold it slightly low and wide, and try golden hour for flattering light.
card.rules_and_safety: The creek is a public waterway with boats working on it, so keep yourself and your phone well back from the water's edge.
card.challenge: Get a lantern in the foreground and an abra crossing the middle of the frame, all in one shot. Bonus points if the water stays level on the gridlines.
card.good_to_know: Dubai Creek is a natural saltwater inlet that runs about 14 km inland from the Persian Gulf, and it gave the city its first harbour. It split the old city into Bur Dubai and Deira, and wooden abras still ferry people between them. Dredging began in the early 1960s, and Al Maktoum Bridge, the first crossing between the two banks, opened in 1963.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Al Seef Park, on the creekside promenade along the Al Seef waterfront. Face the water so the old-style buildings and lanterns are close in front of you and the abras cross behind them.

card.hook: Here's a fun trick: one shot, two Dubais. Old coral-stone walls on your side, and the modern skyline waiting across the water on the other.
card.stand_here: Head for Saeed Al Maktoum House on the Dubai Creek waterfront in Al Shindagha. The phone icon sits at the middle of the building, so once you're at the house you're in the right place. Go up to the terraces or the majlis and face the Creek.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x on the terraces and in the majlis to squeeze in the Creek, the skyline and the terrace framing together. Use 1x for the main view across the water. Then try 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the carved upper windows, the wind towers, or buildings on the far bank.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines to keep the far bank level, use the terrace openings as a frame, then tap the skyline and drag brightness down a touch if the sky is glaring.
card.best_time: Go early morning or late afternoon, when the low sun warms the coral-stone walls. Museum visiting times decide when you can reach the terraces, so check the official site first.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x and hold the phone a little higher than your face. That squeezes in more of the old building behind your shoulder, and your smile still gets top billing.
card.rules_and_safety: The upper terraces and majlis are reached through the museum, so check the official site for opening times and entry details. Photography may be limited in some rooms inside, so keep an eye out for signs.
card.challenge: Find a terrace opening that frames the Creek like a picture frame, then see if you can catch a bit of the skyline inside it with the horizon dead straight.
card.good_to_know: The house was built around 1896 as the seat of the Al Maktoum family. Sheikh Saeed bin Maktoum Al Maktoum, a former ruler of Dubai, lived here until his death in 1958. Today it's a museum of old Dubai with nine wings, covering 3,600 square metres, so there's plenty to look at.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Saeed Al Maktoum House on the Dubai Creek waterfront in Al Shindagha. The phone icon sits at the middle of the building, so once you're at the house you're in the right place. Go up to the terraces or the majlis and face the Creek.

card.hook: Cross the road and Jumeirah Mosque lines itself up for you: a dome in the middle, a minaret on each side and nothing but open sky behind. It's the classic Dubai postcard, and it's very easy to take.
card.stand_here: Stand on Jumeirah Beach Road, straight across from the mosque's street-facing front, and face it square-on. The sign might say Jumeirah Street instead, so check the street signs when you arrive.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from across the road so the dome and both minarets fit together. If you're tight against the building, try zoom 0.5x and keep the phone level so the minarets don't lean. Zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) is great for the carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the centre of the dome on the middle line with a minaret on each side, and leave a little sky above.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or about an hour before sunset, when the light is softer and warmer on the sandstone.
card.selfie_here: Try the palm-tree side of the mosque, which one travel guide calls a scenic photo spot, or the courtyard where the white front and minarets show (check access to the grounds first). Use the front camera, zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and tuck the mosque in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the pavement of Jumeirah Beach Road and ask them to frame the whole front of the mosque from the street while you stand in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep worshippers out of your pictures, and ask first if you want a close-up of anyone. Leave the selfie stick in your bag and keep your poses dignified rather than goofy. Entry is by guided tour only (none on Fridays), so check the official site if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Take one shot where both minarets are the same size and the dome sits dead centre. Bonus points if it's your most symmetrical photo of the whole trip.
card.good_to_know: The mosque is built of yellow-pink sandstone, and official accounts name Fatimid design as the inspiration. Building began in 1975 and it opened in 1979, a gift from Sheikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum to his son, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum. It holds up to 1,200 worshippers and appeared on the 2003 series of the 500 dirham note.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Jumeirah Beach Road, straight across from the mosque's street-facing front, and face it square-on. The sign might say Jumeirah Street instead, so check the street signs when you arrive.

card.hook: Here the sacks of spice sit right at eye level, so your phone basically does the colour work for you. Even a quick snap looks like you planned it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Deira Old Souk Abra Station landing, a short walk south-east of the souk centre (about 1 minute on foot to the middle of the souk, to the north-west). Face the souk entrance, which looks straight at the landing.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the shopfronts and colourful sacks. Drop to 0.5x to fit the souk entrance, the abra boats and the creek into one shot. For piles of spice up close, try 2x to 5x (it depends on your phone), so you don't have to lean into a stall.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sacks, then slide the picture a touch darker so bright sky or sunlit stalls don't wash out the colours.
card.best_time: Mornings are the pick, especially on weekdays, for softer light and fewer people. Light changes, so be ready to nudge brighter or darker.
card.selfie_here: Try the abra station on the Bur Dubai side of the creek, which looks northeast across the water to the Deira waterfront where the Spice Souk is. Use the front camera at 0.5x with your back to the creek and the waterfront over your shoulder. It's a creek-scene spot rather than a souk close-up, so check your frame to see how much of the souk shows.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in the souks, but ask first before photographing people or their goods, and stop if you're asked to. Shopkeepers often object to close-ups that aren't followed by a purchase. Drones aren't practical in this heritage area.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the row of shopfronts on the lower third, and sneak a passing abra boat into the foreground.
card.good_to_know: The Dubai Spice Souk is a traditional market in Deira, with narrow lanes of open and covered shops. It sits on Baniyas Street in Al Ras, next to the Gold Souk. Along with spices, herbs and frankincense, shops sell tea, textiles and rugs, and most buying is done by haggling.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Deira Old Souk Abra Station landing, a short walk south-east of the souk centre (about 1 minute on foot to the middle of the souk, to the north-west). Face the souk entrance, which looks straight at the landing.

card.hook: Picture narrow lanes, low sand-coloured walls and a stranger strolling through your shot just as you tap the button. That's Al Fahidi, and it's half the fun.
card.stand_here: Stand at Al Fahidi Fort, out on the surrounding square, and face the fort so the low sand-coloured walls of the restored neighbourhood sit around it. It's the oldest surviving building in Dubai, so it's an easy first photo.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the fort and wider views. Switch to zoom 0.5x in the tight lanes, then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for windows and wall details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a sunlit wall, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sandy walls keep their detail and don't turn white.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and cooler walking. Go early and you'll also dodge the busiest lanes.
card.selfie_here: Try the decorated wall at the Arabic Calligraphy House (Dar Al Khatt Alarabi), 4 Al Mussalla Street. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and stand close so the wall fills the space behind you. It's an older tip, so if the wall looks different, pick another pretty wall nearby.
card.rules_and_safety: The fort's museum is closed for restoration, so plan on outside views only. Ask before you photograph people, and keep it quiet around residential areas. Some alleys have no shade, so bring sun protection and water.
card.challenge: Find one Islamic-style window, fill the whole frame with it, and see if you can snap it before a stranger wanders past.
card.good_to_know: Al Fahidi, also called Al Bastakiya, dates back to the 1890s and was built largely by well-off Persian merchants. The name comes from the southern Iranian town of Bastak. About half of it was cleared in the 1980s, and a 1989 demolition order was cancelled after British architect Rayner Otter campaigned to save it. Restoration began in 2005.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Al Fahidi Fort, out on the surrounding square, and face the fort so the low sand-coloured walls of the restored neighbourhood sit around it. It's the oldest surviving building in Dubai, so it's an easy first photo.

card.hook: Picture a giant white page, curling up at the edges, with seven pens standing guard in front of it. That's the Etihad Museum, and from the lawn it looks wonderfully clean: white curves, big sky, hardly any clutter.
card.stand_here: Stand on the outdoor lawn in front of the Etihad Museum, about 1.6 km north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. From here you can see the curved white roof as a whole.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole building in. If you're close and the roofline won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for details like the columns and the edge of the roof.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the roof up with the horizontal lines, then tap the white wall and nudge it a little darker so the white keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is soft and flatters white buildings. Strong midday sun can wash out all those lovely curves.
card.selfie_here: Head to the flagpole that rises above the reflecting pool on the grounds next to Union House. Guides call it the most photographed spot on the property. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more of the scene in, and have the flagpole and sky behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash is banned in rooms that hold original documents. Photo rules inside can vary, so check the museum's official site before you go, and treat the outdoor views as your reliable choice.
card.challenge: Walk once around the outside and take a photo every time the roofline changes shape. Which one is your favourite?
card.good_to_know: The museum stands on the site where the rulers signed the union declaration, and where the first national flag was raised, on 2 December 1971. The round Union House, where the signing happened, is now part of the complex and was formerly known as the Jumeirah Guesthouse. The building is shaped like a manuscript, and its seven columns stand for the pens used to sign the declaration.
